section.title: The LORD's Anger Against Israel
section.sectionRationale: The judgment oracles reach their most severe pitch. Ephraim, once exalted, died through Baal; prosperity bred pride and forgetfulness, so God will meet them like a lion and a bear. Yet even at the darkest, a startling promise flashes out: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol, the verse Paul takes up in the triumph over death.
section.thesis: Because Israel forgot the God who alone is Savior and turned to idols and kings, judgment falls like a wild beast; yet the same God who declares there is no Savior besides Me announces He will ransom His people from the power of death.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the idols that brought death and God the only Savior; the pride of the well-fed and the beast of judgment; and the ransom from Sheol shining amid a final word of wrath on Samaria.

units.label: Idols that bring death, a Savior forgotten
units.note: no God and no Savior besides Me

verses.text: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.

Now they sin more and more and make for themselves cast images, idols skillfully made from their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen. People say of them, “They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!”
Therefore they will be like the morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes, like chaff blown from a threshing floor, like smoke through an open window.
Yet I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt; you know no God but Me, for there is no {{yasha|Savior}} besides Me.

units.label: Pride of the well-fed, the beast of judgment

verses.text: I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought.
When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me.
So like a lion I will pounce on them; like a leopard I will lurk by the path.
Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them, and I will tear open their chests. There I will devour them like a lion, like a wild beast tearing them apart.

units.label: Ransomed from the power of death
units.note: where, O Death, is your sting?

verses.text: You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me, against your helper.
Where is your king now to save you in all your cities, and the rulers to whom you said, “Give me a king and princes”?
So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away.
The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is stored up.
Labor pains come upon him, but he is an unwise son. When the time arrives, he fails to present himself at the opening of the womb.

I will {{padah|ransom}} them from the power of {{sheol|Sheol}}; I will {{gaal|redeem}} them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting? Compassion is hidden from My eyes.

Although he flourishes among his brothers, an east wind will come, a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert. His fountain will fail, and his spring will run dry. The wind will plunder his treasury of every precious article.
Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword; their little ones will be dashed to pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open.

yasha.gloss: To save, to deliver, to rescue; the root behind the words for Savior and salvation, and behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves. In verse 4 God insists there is no Savior besides Me, exposing the folly of trusting idols and kings, and pointing to the salvation He alone gives, fulfilled in Christ.

padah.gloss: To ransom, to redeem by paying a price, to buy back. In verse 14 God promises to ransom His people from the power of Sheol, a stunning pledge of rescue from death itself, taken up by Paul in the triumph of resurrection over the grave.

sheol.gloss: The grave, the realm of the dead, the pit. It pictures the power of death that swallows all people. God's promise to ransom His people from the power of Sheol declares His mastery over death, the very power Christ breaks in His resurrection.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer, to buy back what is lost and reclaim one's own. Alongside padah in verse 14, gaal stresses that God rescues His people as their near kinsman, a role fulfilled when Christ becomes our brother and redeems us from Death itself.

basic.context: This is the sternest chapter in Hosea. Ephraim was once honored, but idolatry killed it spiritually. The people keep making silver idols and even kiss calf images. God reminds them that He alone has been their God since Egypt, and there is no Savior besides Him. But when they grew full and comfortable, they became proud and forgot Him, so He will come against them like a lion, a leopard, and a bear. Their kings cannot save them. And yet, in the middle of the darkness, God flashes out a promise: I will ransom them from the power of the grave, and He taunts Death itself.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter's severity is real covenant judgment, climaxing in the horror of verse 16. Verse 14 is famously double-edged in Hebrew and can be read as promise or as taunt; Paul settles its ultimate meaning by quoting it as the shout of resurrection triumph. Read canonically, the ransom from death is God's last word over His people, even though wrath falls in history.
basic.originalLanguages: God declares there is no yasha, Savior, besides Him, the root behind the name Jesus. Then, astonishingly, He promises to padah, ransom, and gaal, redeem, His people from sheol, the grave, and from Death. Savior, ransom, kinsman-redeemer, and the grave defeated: this is the vocabulary of the gospel breaking into the darkest oracle.
basic.typology: God as the only Savior points directly to Jesus, whose name means the LORD saves. The promise to ransom and redeem from Sheol and Death is fulfilled in Christ's resurrection, which Paul proclaims by quoting this very verse. The unwise son who will not come forth from the womb points by contrast to Christ, the wise Son who comes forth from the tomb in resurrection life.
basic.christ: God says there is no Savior besides Me, and the New Testament names that Savior Jesus, the LORD who saves. The most electrifying line, I will ransom them from the power of Sheol, I will redeem them from Death, is taken up by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15, where the taunt Where, O Death, is your sting becomes the church's resurrection song. What Hosea announces God will do, Christ accomplishes: by His own death and rising He ransoms His people from the grave and disarms Death forever. The wrath that falls in this chapter is real, and Christ absorbs it, so that the promise of ransom stands as God's final word.
basic.god: God is the sole Savior, and this chapter shows how jealously He guards that truth, for idols and kings only bring death. He is holy and just; forgetfulness bred by comfort provokes His fierce anger, pictured as a wounded, predatory beast. Yet at the same moment He reveals a mercy that reaches past the grave itself, promising to ransom His people from death. His justice and His saving love meet here in tension that only the cross and empty tomb resolve.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:55 quotes Hosea's taunt over death in the triumph of resurrection. Matthew 1:21 names Jesus, for He will save His people. Acts 4:12 declares there is salvation in no one else.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 13 shows a people killed by idolatry and pride, facing the beast of judgment, yet hearing the promise of ransom from the grave. The Bible answers this in Christ, the only Savior, who by His resurrection ransoms His people from Sheol and turns the taunt of Death into the shout of victory.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a descent that is interrupted. It opens in verse 1 with a short obituary: Ephraim spoke and others trembled, then he sinned through Baal and died. Everything after that is an explanation of how a nation once so full of life came to be a corpse. Verses 1 to 3 give the cause and the result in a single breath, guilt through idols and then the four vanishing pictures of mist, dew, chaff and smoke. Verses 4 to 8 turn on a memory, the God who knew Israel in the desert, and the beasts that now stalk the path. Verses 9 to 11 turn on the failure of kings. Verses 12 to 14 gather up the guilt, show Ephraim as a child who cannot be born, and then break into the taunt to Death. Verses 15 and 16 close with the east wind and the sword.

Notice how the images of the chapter keep working at one thing, which is the swiftness and completeness of loss. Mist, dew, chaff and smoke are things that are present one minute and absent the next. The lion, leopard and bear are predators that strike from hiding. The east wind dries up a spring. The woman in labour is trapped at the moment of crisis. In every case something that should have given life ends up giving death.

The chapter also echoes the earlier oracles on purpose. The mist and the early dew come straight from Hosea 6:4, where God complained that Israel's loyalty was exactly that, and here the same pictures describe Israel itself. The lion of verse 7 returns the lion of Hosea 5:14. The reminder of the exodus in verse 4 repeats the opening words of Hosea 12:9. The chapter sits at the end of the long indictment of chapters 4 to 13, and the stark tone of its close is the reason the gentler chapter 14 hits so strongly.

The most striking literary feature is where verse 14 falls. It sits between the stored up sin of verse 12 and the east wind of verse 15, and it is wrapped on both sides by judgment. Whatever the verse means, the author has set it down in the middle of a sentence of death.
context.historical:
Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, and Hosea uses its name for the whole nation. Jeroboam, who first led the north away from David's house, was an Ephraimite, 1 Kings 11:26, and he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so that no one would need to go up to Jerusalem, 1 Kings 12:28 to 30. The 'trembling' of verse 1 looks back to the days when Ephraim was a tribe that carried weight, when Joshua came from it, Numbers 13:8, and when it received Jacob's blessing in the place of the firstborn, Genesis 48:19. The 'Baal' of that verse is the storm and fertility god of Canaan, whose worship Ahab and Jezebel had pushed with royal power, 1 Kings 16:31 to 33. To kiss the calves was an act of homage. The footnote to verse 2 observes that the line can also be read as men who sacrifice kissing the calves, and 1 Kings 19:18 speaks of mouths that had kissed Baal. The reference to human sacrifice reflects the evil practices that Deuteronomy 12:31 had warned against and that Judah's later kings would also take up.

The setting is the last years of the northern kingdom, before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. The nation fell into a run of rapid coups, and kings were made and murdered within years, 2 Kings 15:8 to 31. Verses 10 and 11 stare at this. The 'king' and 'princes' the people demanded echo 1 Samuel 8:5 to 20, where the elders asked Samuel for a king like the nations, and God told Samuel it was Himself they had rejected, 1 Samuel 8:7. Hosea has already said that the north set up kings without God's consent, Hosea 8:4.

The last verse reads like a war report because it is one. The Assyrian army was known for its brutality, and Israel's own kings had done the same, since Menahem had ripped open the pregnant women of Tiphsah, 2 Kings 15:16. Amos 1:13 uses the same language against Ammon. The east wind of verse 15 would have been familiar to any farmer as the hot desert blast that scorches the crops, and Hosea 12:1 had already said that Ephraim 'pursues the east wind'. The wind is also the direction from which Assyria would come.
context.canonical:
The chapter looks back into the Torah and forward into the gospel. Behind verses 5 and 6 stands the warning of Deuteronomy 8:11 to 14, where Moses told the people that when they ate and were satisfied, when herds multiplied and silver increased, their hearts would grow proud and they would forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt. Hosea shows the warning coming true to the letter. Behind verse 4 stand the first commandments, Exodus 20:2 and 3, and the great claim of Isaiah 43:11, 'there is no Savior but Me,' which Hosea says in almost the same words. Behind the lion and the bear stand the prophet's earlier warning in Hosea 5:14 and the stories of 1 Samuel 17:34 to 37, where lion and bear were the predators a shepherd faced. The wider prophets use the same pairing, Amos 5:19 and Lamentations 3:10, and Daniel's vision of beasts, Daniel 7:4 to 6, gathers lion, bear and leopard together as images of the powers that rule and devour.

Forward from verse 14 the canon moves in two directions. Isaiah 25:8 says of the LORD, 'He will swallow up death forever,' and Paul puts that line beside Hosea in 1 Corinthians 15:54 and 55, where he cites 'Death has been swallowed up in victory' and then 'Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?' The wording is not identical to the Hebrew or to the Septuagint, which the BSB footnote on verse 14 shows, so Paul is using Hosea as a pattern and a voice rather than lifting an exact sentence. Second, Acts 2:24 says God raised Jesus, 'releasing Him from the agony of death,' and the phrase draws on the language of birth pains that Hosea uses of Ephraim in verse 13.

The chapter also stands among the Twelve as the last of Hosea's judgment oracles before the call to return, and its words about idolatry, pride and the king are taken up when Hosea's reader meets Israel's later history.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea meant his hearers to see that their situation was not a mystery. They were prosperous, and the prosperity had made them forget the One who made it. The chapter is a courtroom summary: the charge is idolatry and forgetfulness, the evidence is the silver idols and the sated pride, the witnesses are the kings who cannot save, and the sentence is carried out by lion, leopard, bear and wind. He wanted a comfortable generation to feel how fragile their strength was, as breakable as mist or smoke.

He also meant them to hear a claim about who God is. The reminder of the exodus in verse 4 says that the God now pouncing is the very God who brought them out of Egypt. Judgment is not a different God taking over. It is the same Savior treating the rescued as if they had never been rescued, because they had treated Him as if He had never rescued. The first hearers are driven to a choice between two saviors, the king and the idol on one side and the LORD on the other.

The strange sentence at the heart of the chapter, verse 14, was meant to unsettle. Whether read as an offer or a challenge, it makes the hearer aware that death is not the last thing the LORD has to say, and that His answer to it belongs to Him alone. A people about to go into exile were being taught that the God who struck them was also the only one who could bring them back from the dead.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what God said He would do to a particular nation at a particular point in history. It does not hand believers a recipe for how a nation's fortunes follow its behaviour, and it does not say that every disaster is a judgment on those who suffer it. Hosea was speaking to Israel under the Mosaic covenant, where the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 were written into the terms. Applying verse 16 to any modern people as if God had pledged the same sentence would be reading the covenant into a setting it was not made for.

What carries over is the pattern of the heart. Verse 6 describes a spiritual sequence anyone can fall into: provision, then satisfaction, then pride, then forgetfulness. The warning of Deuteronomy 8 and the example of this chapter teach comfortable believers to be most watchful when they have the least to complain about. The shape of the offer in verse 14 also carries over, in a form the New Testament spells out. It is not that suffering should be borne as deserved, but that the God who alone saves has acted to ransom from death, and that this is what we proclaim.

The violence of verse 16 is recorded, not recommended. The prophet reports what the nations would do as God's instrument. The Bible does not tell the reader to imitate such brutality, and the same prophets condemn it when others commit it, as in Amos 1:13.

debates.question: Is Hosea 13:14 a promise of rescue or a threat?

views.label: A promise of redemption from death
views.case: The BSB reads the verbs as statements: 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death.' Paul takes the verse as the shout of resurrection triumph in 1 Corinthians 15:55, and the word padah is the language of rescue elsewhere, as in Psalm 49:15 where God ransoms the soul from the power of Sheol. On this reading the sudden brightness is Hosea's pattern throughout the book, where judgment is followed by a pledge of restoration, as in Hosea 2:14 and 11:8 to 9.

views.label: Rhetorical questions that expect the answer no
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew can be read as questions, 'Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?' The last line, 'Compassion is hidden from My eyes,' fits a context where verses 12, 13, 15 and 16 are hard. On this reading the Lord is calling on Death and Sheol to bring their plagues and their sting against Ephraim, and the verse is a final threat.

views.label: A promise that waits beyond the sentence
views.case: A third view keeps both. The generation in view will indeed be struck, so that for that generation compassion is hidden, but the verse stands in the text as a pledge for a restored people on the far side of the judgment. Hosea's contemporaries could have heard the threat, while later readers, with the whole book and the resurrection in hand, hear the promise.

debates.bearing: The footnote tells us the ambiguity is real, and a careful reader should say so. What weighs most is the canonical context. Hosea does not end at chapter 13, and the book moves through the sentence to the healing of chapter 14. Paul's use of the verse in 1 Corinthians 15 shows how the apostles read it, as a promise of God to be fulfilled in Christ, even if the immediate point in the prophet's day was a harsh one.

debates.question: Did Hosea have the resurrection of the dead in view?

views.label: Only the national revival of Israel
views.case: Many read the ransom from Sheol as a picture for the survival of the nation after the exile, much as Ezekiel 37 pictures dry bones standing as an army. Hosea 6:2 speaks of being raised on the third day in a similar way. On this reading Paul gives the language a new application.

views.label: A real hope of rising beyond death
views.case: Others say the prophet's words already reach beyond the picture. Isaiah 25:8 and Daniel 12:2 show that Israel's prophets spoke of the end of death and the awakening of the dead, and Hosea's language of ransom from Sheol is closely akin to Psalm 49:15.

views.label: A picture whose depth is seen only in Christ
views.case: Paul, on this view, is not guessing. He reads the national pattern as a shadow of what the Messiah would do on behalf of His people, so that the national resurrection and the bodily resurrection are two stages of the same promise.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken of what Hosea himself grasped, the New Testament authors read the promise as fulfilled when Christ rose, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the verse is held up as a good example of a prophecy whose full sense is clearer after the event. The chapter does not need Hosea to have understood everything for God to have said it.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb 'know' in verses 4 and 5, yada. God says 'you know no God but Me,' and then 'I knew you in the wilderness.' In Hosea, knowing is the language of covenant intimacy, and the lack of it is the root complaint of the whole book, Hosea 4:1 and 6:6. The wording sets two kinds of knowing side by side: Israel's knowledge of God, which has been squeezed out, and God's knowledge of Israel, which has never failed. Amos 3:2 uses the same verb of God's choice of Israel alone. The verb in verse 5 is the same one that describes a husband's knowledge of his wife, which is why the exodus reminder reads as a marriage reminder.

The two verbs of forgetting and filling in verse 6 are a pair. 'Satisfied' is the verb saba, and 'forgot' is shakach. Deuteronomy 8:12 and 14 puts the very same pair of ideas in the same order, which is why many readers hear verse 6 as the warning of Moses arriving. Hosea 2:13 had already said of Israel 'she forgot Me.' The word for 'proud,' literally 'lifted up,' is the same stem as the one in Deuteronomy 8:14, so the descent from satisfaction to elevation to forgetfulness is the Torah's own.

Verse 7 begins 'I will be to them like a lion,' as the Hebrew reads, using the simple verb to be. The picture of God as a beast of prey is unusual, and Hosea 5:14 uses the lion in the same way. In verse 8 the 'bear robbed of her cubs' calls up the proverb that it is better to meet such a bear than a fool in his folly, Proverbs 17:12, and the heart is torn open, an image of exposing the deepest part of a person.

Verse 12 uses two verbs for storing up. 'Bound up' is the verb tsarar, which is also the verb for tying silver in a bag, 2 Kings 5:23, and the second verb is a word for what is hidden away as treasure. The sin of Ephraim is being kept as in a purse, with nothing lost, until the day of reckoning. Job 14:17 uses a similar picture, with transgression sealed up in a bag.

The labour imagery of verse 13 is exact. The 'opening of the womb' is the place where the child must come out. The verb behind 'present himself' is the verb to stand. A child who will not stand at the place of birth will die with the mother. 'Unwise' is lo chakam, the language of the wisdom tradition, where the fool is the one who will not learn.

Finally, notice the Hebrew word 'ehi, which appears at the head of the question in verse 10, 'Where is your king,' and again at the head of both lines in verse 14, 'Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?' The footnote at verse 10 shows that the same sounds can be read as 'I will be,' so that the verse could say 'I will be your King now.' This is the grammatical reason the verse can be heard two ways. The word for 'plagues,' deber, is the word for the pestilence of the fifth plague in Egypt, Exodus 9:3.

typology.type: The womb and the labour that cannot end, Hosea 13:13
typology.fulfillment: Ephraim is pictured as a child who will not come out when the time arrives, so that both life and mother are lost. It sets up a pattern of life blocked by death and by folly. In Christ the picture is turned. Peter says in Acts 2:24 that God raised Him up 'releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' using the old word for birth pangs, as though death itself were the womb. Paul calls Him 'the firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18. Where Ephraim failed to emerge, Christ emerged, and brings many with Him. The type falls short at one point: Ephraim's failure was caused by his own folly, while Christ's emergence was by right.

typology.type: The king given in anger, Hosea 13:10 and 11
typology.fulfillment: Israel asked for a king and God gave one in His wrath, 1 Samuel 8:5 to 7 and Hosea 13:11, and the kings failed to save. The institution then points beyond itself. Hosea himself says that the people will later seek 'David their king,' Hosea 3:5. In Christ the kingship is finally good: He is the King the people could not make, born of David's line, Matthew 1:1. At His trial the title 'King of the Jews' was hung over Him in mockery, Matthew 27:37, yet it was the truth. Those who asked for a king like the nations got one who could not save, and God sent a King who saves by dying. The type falls short because every earlier king was a sinner, and none could ransom his people.

typology.type: Ransom from Sheol, the way Jonah was brought up, Hosea 13:14
typology.fulfillment: Hosea's promise that God will ransom from the power of Sheol has a pattern in Jonah, who cried 'from the belly of Sheol' and was brought up from the pit, Jonah 2:2 and 6. Jesus claims that pattern for Himself when He says that as Jonah was in the great fish three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40. The escalation is that Jonah was delivered himself, while Christ goes into death on behalf of others and brings them out with Him, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The pattern is partial: Jonah did not die for anyone, and his rescue won no one else's.

typology.type: Wilderness knowledge and pasture forgetfulness, Hosea 13:5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: Israel was known in the desert and forgot in the pasture. The wilderness is the school of dependence, and Deuteronomy 8:3 says God fed them with manna to teach that man lives by every word from His mouth. Jesus takes the same wilderness and hunger and does not fall, Matthew 4:1 to 4, quoting that verse. He is the true Israel who remembers in the desert, and who tells His followers that He is the bread that came down from heaven, John 6:35. The type falls short because Israel's wilderness story ends in forgetting, while Christ's does not.

study.christ:
The chapter begins to lead to Christ in its own insistence that there is no Savior but the LORD. Verse 4 is almost a quotation of Isaiah 43:11, and the New Testament does not soften this claim when it applies the title of Savior to Jesus. Paul writes of 'our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,' Titus 2:13, and Peter says there is salvation in no one else, Acts 4:12. The jealous exclusivity of Hosea 13:4 is the soil in which the confession that Jesus is Lord grows. Either Jesus is the God who alone saves, or the New Testament has joined what the prophet forbids.

The chapter leads to Christ by the ransom of verse 14. The two verbs, padah and gaal, are the vocabulary of the exodus and of the kinsman who buys back what has been lost, and the New Testament takes both up. Jesus says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Paul says He redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The pledge is not just that death will be reversed, but that there is a price and a Person who pays it. Hebrews 2:14 and 15 reads the work as breaking the one who holds the power of death and setting free those who were in bondage by fear of it.

It leads to Christ by the voice of Paul. In 1 Corinthians 15:54 and 55 he gathers Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 into a single song, 'Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?' He then adds, 'The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law,' verse 56. That comment brings the chapter's two halves together, because the sin stored up in verse 12 is the sting that Death holds, and it is exactly that sting that Christ has taken into Himself. Where Hosea heard God holding back compassion, Paul hears God giving thanks 'who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ,' verse 57.

It also leads to Christ by contrast with the beasts. The lion of Hosea is God, and the wrath He pictures is not a different thing from the wrath that fell on the Son. The Lamb who was slain is also called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Revelation 5:5 and 6, and He has taken what the sin of Ephraim deserved. Verse 8 describes the tearing of the chest, and the Servant was 'pierced for our transgressions,' Isaiah 53:5.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Hosea 13 is first a hard word to a real nation, and it is not a puzzle about Jesus. The strength of the christological link is that the New Testament itself uses verse 14, and that the verse's themes of sole saviorhood, ransom and conquest over Death are the heart of what Christ did. The chapter supplies the problem, a people dead in their idolatry and sin, and the apostles supply the name of the one who answered it.
study.god:
This chapter shows the LORD as the God who remembers. The accusation is mostly about what Israel forgot, and the line that anchors everything is 'I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought,' verse 5. Other gods are made by craftsmen and have to be carried. The LORD is the one who has known Israel from before she was a nation, and His knowledge is the contrast to her forgetting. A God who knows His people in the desert is a God whose anger is not detached from love, because it is the anger of someone who remembers what He did for them.

It shows Him as the only Savior, and this is stated as a fact about the universe rather than a boast. Verse 4 says there is no Savior besides Him, and the rest of the chapter proves it from the opposite side. Idols dissolve like smoke, kings cannot rescue in all the cities, and the one who is left to do the saving is the LORD. The oneness of God is shown here in practical terms: He alone can be turned to when death comes.

It shows Him as sovereign over history and over enemies. The lion, leopard and bear and the east wind are His own agents, and verse 15 says 'a wind from the LORD.' The Assyrians who come are, in the text, the instruments of a God who is not outmaneuvered by empires. This is hard to hear and is meant to be. It does not make God the author of evil, because the chapter blames Ephraim throughout. It teaches that human cruelty can be taken up into a divine verdict that Israel's own guilt called for, and that the judge is not at the mercy of events.

It shows a God whose emotions are real and strong. He gave the king 'in My anger' and took him away 'in My wrath,' verse 11. He is 'like a bear robbed of her cubs,' a picture of fierce protective love turned on those who betray it. This is not the cold anger of a bureaucrat. The tension in the chapter is that the same God says in Hosea 11:8 that His heart is turned within Him, and here says that compassion is hidden from His eyes. Both are true at the same time in the text, and Scripture does not resolve them by flattening either.

It shows a God who is jealous in the right way. The first commandments prohibit other gods because He is the only source of life, not because He is a rival in a contest. To love Israel meant to refuse to share her.

For worship, this chapter teaches us to be on guard exactly when the table is full, and to take the discipline of pasture seriously. It teaches us to ask 'who is saving me?' and to say the answer aloud. And it gives us in verse 14 something to sing at funerals, where the question 'where is your sting' is addressed to the enemy in the confidence that the God who alone ransoms is also the one who has begun to do it.

crossReferences.note: God's earlier complaint that Israel's loyalty was like a morning mist and the early dew that vanishes. In Hosea 13:3 the same two images are turned on Israel herself. What she offered God, that is what she will become, a fleeting thing that disappears.

Moses warned that when the people ate and were satisfied and their herds and silver multiplied, their hearts would grow proud and they would forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt. Hosea 13:6 is the warning arriving word for word as history, so that the prophet is applying Torah, not inventing a new charge.

The LORD says, 'I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.' Hosea 13:4 makes the same claim with the same title. The claim is meant to sink the hope of every other helper, whether an idol, an alliance or a king.

God tells Samuel the people have not rejected the prophet, but have rejected Him as their king. Verses 10 and 11 of Hosea look back to this day. Their kings became the thing they trusted instead of Him, and the gift of a king in anger recalls how the request was met.

God says He is like a lion to Ephraim and a young lion to Judah, who will tear them to pieces and carry them off where no one can rescue. Chapter 13 expands that lion into a lion, leopard and bear, and shows that nothing has changed since the first warning.

The great turn of the book, where God asks how He could give Ephraim up and says His compassion is stirred. Set beside 13:14, where compassion is hidden, it shows the tension between wrath and mercy that Hosea holds without resolving until the final chapter.

Paul gathers Isaiah and Hosea into the song of resurrection victory, 'Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?' He uses the taunt of Hosea 13:14 as God's last word, and he identifies the day when it will be sung.

'He will swallow up death forever.' Paul sets this beside Hosea in 1 Corinthians 15. Isaiah supplies the end of death, Hosea supplies the voice that taunts it, and both are taken up by Paul as the work of Christ.

The psalmist says God will redeem his soul from the power of Sheol. The same sort of verb and noun as Hosea 13:14 appears here, showing that the hope of being ransomed from the grave was already alive in Israel's worship, and not first heard in Hosea.

Peter says God raised Jesus, releasing Him from the agony of death, because death could not hold Him. The word for agony is a word for birth pains, so Peter's account of the resurrection echoes the labour imagery of Hosea 13:13, with the difference that this child does come out.

Through His own death the Son destroyed the one who holds the power of death and freed those who were enslaved all their lives by fear of it. It spells out how the ransom of Hosea 13:14 is paid, which is by the death and rising of a man who shared our flesh.

Menahem ripped open the pregnant women of Tiphsah. The language is close to the final verse of Hosea 13, and shows that the judgment promised matched the cruelty Israel's own kings had practised, so that the violence of verse 16 is no arbitrary excess.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question the Bible has been asking since the exodus: what happens when God's rescued people turn out to be a people who forget being rescued? Genesis showed man in a garden of plenty choosing a lie, and Deuteronomy showed Israel warned that plenty would do the same to them. Hosea 13 is where the warning comes true. The same pattern, gifts received and giver forgotten, runs through Judges, where each generation falls into the cycle of idols and oppression, and through the kings, where the first king is requested in 1 Samuel 8 and the northern line ends in Hoshea. The chapter stands at the end of that road, and its tone is that of a verdict.

What it sets up is the long exile and the longer wait. The sentence of the chapter was carried out in 722 BC, when Samaria fell and her people were scattered, 2 Kings 17:5 to 6. The ten tribes disappear from the story as a nation. And yet verse 14 is left standing in the text like a stake driven into the ground ahead of the coming flood. The prophets after Hosea take up the same promise: Isaiah says that God will swallow up death forever, Isaiah 25:8, Ezekiel sees the dry bones live, Ezekiel 37:12, and Daniel is told that many who sleep in the dust will awake, Daniel 12:2.

The story comes to rest in Christ, who is the answer to the question 'who can save?' that the whole chapter is asking. Israel's kings could not, her idols could not, her sacrifices could not. Jesus walks into the place where Death keeps its plagues, and comes out. Paul says that Christ has been raised, 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The ransom of Hosea is the first harvest of a field that is still being gathered.

The new creation is where verse 14 is finally spoken without any qualification. John hears that there will be no more death or mourning, and sees Death and Hades thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:14 and 21:4. The beasts that devoured Ephraim are gone, and the wind from the desert has dried no spring, for the river of the water of life flows from the throne, Revelation 22:1. The people who forgot their God will see His face and will not forget again.

quiz.q: What does God insist about Himself in verse 4?

options.text: He alone is God and Savior; there is no Savior besides Him.
options.note: Verse 4 declares there is no Savior besides the LORD.

options.text: That idols can save if made well enough.
options.note: The chapter exposes idols as bringing death, not salvation.

options.text: That kings are the true saviors of Israel.
options.note: Their kings cannot save them, verse 10.

options.text: That salvation comes from Assyria.
options.note: God alone is Savior; Assyria brings judgment.

quiz.q: What made Israel forget God, according to verse 6?

options.text: When they were satisfied and full, their hearts became proud and they forgot Him.
options.note: Comfort bred pride and forgetfulness, verse 6.

options.text: Severe famine and hardship.
options.note: It was fullness, not famine, that led them astray here.

options.text: Being conquered too early.
options.note: The forgetting came in prosperity, before the conquest.

options.text: Never having known God at all.
options.note: God knew them in the wilderness; they forgot a God they knew.

quiz.q: How does Paul use verse 14 in the New Testament?

options.text: He quotes Where, O Death, is your sting as the church's cry of resurrection victory in Christ.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:55 makes it the shout of triumph over death.

options.text: He never refers to it.
options.note: Paul quotes it directly in 1 Corinthians 15.

options.text: He uses it to teach that death always wins.
options.note: He uses it to proclaim death defeated in Christ.

options.text: He uses it to forbid mourning.
options.note: He uses it to celebrate resurrection victory over death.

quiz.q: How does the promise to ransom from Sheol point to Christ?

options.text: It is fulfilled in Christ's resurrection, by which He ransoms His people from the grave and disarms death.
options.note: Christ accomplishes the ransom Hosea announces, 1 Corinthians 15.

options.text: It means no believer ever physically dies.
options.note: It means death is defeated and cannot hold God's people, not that they never die.

options.text: It refers only to escaping the Assyrians.
options.note: The language reaches past political rescue to victory over death itself.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: Paul ties it directly to Christ's resurrection.

quiz.q: How do God's severe wrath and His ransom promise fit together?

options.text: Both are real, and they are finally reconciled at the cross and empty tomb, where justice and saving love meet.
options.note: The tension of chapter 13 is resolved in Christ.

options.text: The wrath cancels the promise entirely.
options.note: Paul shows the ransom promise stands and triumphs in Christ.

options.text: The promise proves the wrath was never real.
options.note: The wrath is real; Christ bears it so the promise stands.

options.text: They cannot both be true in any sense.
options.note: Both are true and meet in the crucified and risen Christ.

questions: Comfort and fullness led Israel to forget God. How might your own seasons of ease quietly dull your dependence on the Lord?
God insists there is no Savior besides Him. What lesser saviors, whether people, plans, or possessions, are you tempted to trust for rescue?
In the darkest chapter God promises to ransom His people from the grave. How does the hope of resurrection change the way you face death and loss?
Paul turned verse 14 into a shout of victory over death. How can you make Where, O Death, is your sting a real song of hope in your own trials?
Israel's idols brought death, but Christ brings life. What idol do you need to lay down in order to cling to the only Savior?

translationNotes.note: They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves may also be rendered the men who sacrifice kiss the calves, compare 1 Kings 19:18.
Where is your king now may also be rendered Shall I be your King now, a play on Israel's demand for a human king.

The Hebrew can be read as promise or as a taunt summoning judgment; the Septuagint reads Where, O Death, is your penalty? Where, O Hades, is your sting? and this is cited in 1 Corinthians 15:55 as resurrection victory.
